doc.title: Donn Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 6, 2009

title: Faculty leniency and Dean Tolles
summary: Sympathetic professors and Dean Tolles's warning about grades at a fraternity cocktail party.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: I’m curious as to your relationship, the band in general, with the college. Was there a relationship? Did you have anything to do with the music department?

No not really. We were pretty much on our own. I will say that a lot of the faculty were sympathetic to our schedule if you will. I remember in a couple of instances having an assignment due on Monday and to go to the professor and say, you know, the band. And he’d say okay, turn it in Tuesday. And that was great, to get that kind of leniency. And Dean Tolles was very sympathetic, and some of the other professors thought well this is a good thing for the school, even though these kids are on the brink of ruin. Except Emerson was a very bright guy. I think that if he said Donn is going to go play someplace then they kind of let us. But I think that may have had something to do with how I got through this place, was having a sympathetic ear among the faculty and including the dean. In fact, I remember right after I joined the band and we started playing around and I believe it was a winter party, February of 1965, and Dean Tolles came over along with most of the faculty for a cocktail party at the Alpha Delta house which was kind of a tradition. And I remember the description, I don’t know if you heard Phil Mead’s speech today, but he was talking about the suit he always wore, and he was in a rumpled tie and a rumpled shirt and everything. And I remember he was standing there with some kind of liquid in his left hand and a cigarette in his right hand, and the ashes dribbling down his tie. And he says, “Donn, you know, your grades aren’t what they should be. I really think you ought to stop this music business.” And I said, “Well, Dean, you know, I’m on scholarship. I understand that I have to keep my grades up but also I am working at the house as a waiter, and so I need that little bit of money.” And he said, “Well if you have a problem come and see me.” Well I never had to. But I think he kept an eye on me, which he did for everybody, as everybody knows. He was a friend.
